query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of boron to a refractory high‐entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature yield strength by strengthening grain boundary cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase body‐centered cubic refractory high‐entropy alloy such as MoNbTaVW, as prepared by high-temperature homogenization.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with a small (e.g., 0.1–0.5 at.%) concentration of boron during alloy fabrication.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective for alloys operating under extreme environments, with mechanical performance evaluated via high-temperature compression tests at around 1600°C (e.g., in applications like aerospace engine components or nuclear reactor internals).
generation.mechanism: Boron is proposed to segregate to and bond at the grain boundaries, thereby enhancing their cohesion. This strengthened boundary network is expected to delay the onset of grain-boundary weakening and improve the activation of edge dislocation modes at elevated temperatures, leading to an overall increase in yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength at 1600°C (with an improvement possibly on the order of ~10-20% or more over the baseline of approximately 477 MPa, although the exact magnitude is uncertain) relative to the undoped MoNbTaVW alloy.
generation.baseline: The undoped refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaVW) that typically exhibits a yield strength of around 477 MPa at 1600°C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is specifically targeted at refractory high-entropy alloys with a single-phase body-centered cubic structure subjected to extreme high-temperature conditions (~1600°C). It may not hold for alloys with different phase structures or under significantly different service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement magnitude is uncertain and may depend on the precise doping level, processing conditions, and alloy composition; further experimental calibration is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples with the same base composition and processing conditions. One set will be undoped (baseline MoNbTaVW) and the other set will be doped with 0.1–0.5 at.% boron. Both sets should undergo identical homogenization treatments (e.g., 2100°C for 2 hours followed by air cooling) and be formed into test specimens. Conduct high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C to measure yield strength.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain boundary structure and potential boride formation) via SEM/TEM
Phase verification via XRD to ensure single-phase BCC structure remains intact
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant increase in yield strength at 1600°C compared to the undoped baseline samples, or if microstructural analysis indicates detrimental changes such as phase instability or embrittlement, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
ABSTRACTOver 150 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been proposed in the last decade. Early alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW still show an unparalleled yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 1600°C. However, RHEAs with even elevated high-temperature strength are necessary in aerospace vehicles and nuclear reactors to cope with advanced technology in the future. Here, solid-solution strengthening calculation and melting point prediction are combined to design single-phase RHEA for attaining ultrahigh strength at 1600°C. The results show that Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW alloys after fully homogeneous treatment at 2100°C for 2 h reveal a homogenous body-centered cubic phase. HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa). It is found that a plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C, which is important for raising the strength level of RHEAs at high temperatures. This strengthening mechanism is explained with the change of deformation mode from screw to edge dislocations, which contributes an edge-dislocation-induced strength. A similar alloy design strategy could be applied to develop more RH

After the first development of RHEAs in 2010, over 150 kinds of compositions have been reported, with their potential for use in high-temperature applications such as gas turbine engines and rocket nozzles. Various studies focused on ductility enhancement [,], better oxidation resistance [], and nuclear reactor material applications [,]. According to a review by Senkov et al. [], the only alloys to pass high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C were MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW. The main reason for the difficulty to perform compression tests at extremely high temperatures is the lack of suitable material as a jig material that provides high strength at extremely high temperatures. Recently, Wang et al. strengthened the grain boundary of an MoNbTaW-refractory high-entropy alloy through doping with B or C in trace amount, which simultaneously increases room-temperature strength and toughness []. This study provides a good strategy to increase the ductility of RHEAs by doping suitable elements.
